# Building 4410: Division 26 project specifications (final submittal)

You are the electrical Designer of Record at Harlan Sato Engineers LLC, the architect-engineer for the new Company
Operations Facility, Building 4410, at Fort Calder, an Army design-bid-build project. The electrical design is
complete and coordinated in a building information model. Your task order is to produce the **Division 26 project
specifications** that tell the general contractor and the electrical contractor what to buy and how to install and
test it, edited from the Unified Facilities Guide Specifications to this project's criteria, owner requirements and
installation standard, together with the electrical design basis the specifications rest on.

The project documents are in this workspace: the A/E scope of work and design directives, the transmittal log and
design review comments, the Owner's Project Requirements, the installation electrical design standard, the drawings
and schedules, the electrical coordination model, the utility service data, the calculation basis memoranda, product
data and photometric files, the governing criteria and federal regulations, and the guide specification library. Some
folders hold superseded revisions or material from other agencies; the scope of work and the transmittal log say what
is current and what governs. The NFPA 70 text is not provided.

## What to deliver

`output/submission.zip` containing:

1. `specs/`: **one `.docx` per Division 26 section this task order delivers**, numbered and titled as the
   corresponding Unified Facilities Guide Specification, each a finished project section tailored from that guide
   specification. Edit the guide specification rather than writing sections from scratch: a document that does not
   retain the guide specification's text is not treated as a project section. The scope of work says which sections
   this task order delivers; sections delivered under another task order are neither required nor penalised.
2. `design_basis.xlsx`: the electrical design basis workbook, with these sheets (header in row 1, one record per
   row; extra columns are ignored):

| sheet | columns |
|---|---|
| `Sections` | `number`, `title`, `basis` (why the section is in the project) |
| `Feeders` | `feeder`, `route_length_ft`, `sets`, `size`, `raceway_in`, `vd_pct`, `fill_pct`: one row per feeder and service run on the one-line diagram |
| `ShortCircuit` | `bus`, `voltage_v`, `available_fault_ka`, `specified_rating_ka`: one row per switchboard, panelboard and transfer switch bus on the one-line diagram |
| `Photometric` | `space`, `luminaire_type`, `quantity`, `avg_maintained_fc`, `min_fc`, `uniformity`, `lpd_w_ft2`: one row per interior space in the coordination model |
| `StepLoad` | `step`, `loads`, `step_kva_start`, `voltage_dip_pct`, `recovery_s`: one row per load step, in the order the loads are placed on the engine-generator |
| `Register` | `req_id`, `document` (number/title, with revision or change where there are several), `clause` (paragraph, table, note or row), `requirement`, `value` (the governing number or choice), `applies_to` (section numbers) |
| `Findings` | `finding_id`, `document`, `location`, `defect`, `correction`: errors or inconsistencies you found in the furnished documents and how you resolved them |

## Section format

Each section document must read, as plain paragraphs of text:

- `SECTION nn nn nn` (the section number), the section title, and the section date line;
- `PART 1   GENERAL`, `PART 2   PRODUCTS`, `PART 3   EXECUTION` (a part without content reads `Not used.`);
- articles numbered as typed text, `1.1 REFERENCES`, `1.2 ...`, with upper-case titles; lower-level paragraphs
  `1.2.1 Title`; list items `a.`, `(1)`, `(a)`, `1.`;
- `-- End of Section --` as the last paragraph.

Numbering, list markers and section headings must be literal text in the paragraphs; automatic Word list numbering is
not read. Only paragraph text is read (tables in a section are read cell by cell as paragraphs). Any tool that writes a
valid `.docx` (WordprocessingML package) is fine; no word processor is installed in this workspace, and a `.docx` can be
written with the Python standard library (`zipfile` plus the three required parts: `[Content_Types].xml`, `_rels/.rels`,
`word/document.xml`). No BIM or photometric toolkit is installed either; the coordination model and the photometric
files are text formats and can be parsed with the standard library.

## How the package is judged

Each delivered section is judged as one item against requirements recomputed from the project documents,
independently of wording; values are compared after unit conversion. The design-basis sheets are judged by re-running
the calculations against the design you declare, and the numbers you report are checked against that re-run. A section
with an unresolved choice, or whose design is unsafe or unbuildable, fails a hard requirement family.
Specifications are performance-based and must not be more restrictive than the governing requirement
(FAR 11.002(a)(1)(ii)); a design that meets every limit without over-providing earns the most objective credit. A hard
governing requirement that a section's design rests on and that is missing from your `Register` fails one more hard
family of that section. Each section scores `0.4·p + 0.6·[h = 1]·O`, where `p` is the weighted fraction of the section's
requirement families passed, `h` the weighted fraction of its hard families passed (`[h = 1]` is 1 when every hard
family passes, else 0), and `O` its over-specification credit: a failed hard family zeroes the `O` term.
There is no required number of rows on the `Register` and `Findings` sheets. Defects in the furnished documents and in
the furnished design are scored, so a defect you find and correct belongs on `Findings`, with the correction you made.


## Verifier access (blind variant)

No verifier, oracle, or evaluation data of any kind is available in this workspace; the
only checks you can run are the ones you build yourself. Work from the brief and the
documents alone and submit your best final deliverable; it will be graded offline by the
frozen verifier on held-out instances.

1.3 Scope of this task order. Prepare the Division 26 project specification sections listed in 3.9, and the electrical design basis workbook, for the final (100 %) submittal.

Company Operations Facility (COF), Building 4410, Fort Calder, Georgia. Prepared by Fort Calder Directorate of Public Works for the using unit. Revision B, 30 June 2026.
1 Project description
Two-story company operations facility: administrative offices, company storage, a training room (Room 140), a staff duty desk (Room 101) and a communications room (Room 116).
4 Environmental and operating requirements
4.3 Electrical rooms are conditioned; maximum 85 F.
5 Electrical systems
5.1 Conductors: copper for all feeders and branch circuits.
5.2 Switchboard: provide energy-reducing maintenance switching with local status indicator as the arc energy reduction method for the main breaker.
5.3 Dry-type transformers: meet the 10 CFR 431.196(a)(3) efficiency levels that apply to units manufactured on or after April 23, 2029, regardless of the manufacture date. Additional overload capacity is required for the communications transformer T-C1 (nonlinear electronic loads); no additional overload capacity is required for the other transformers. 5.4 Communications Room 116 houses sensitive electronic equipment: provide cascaded surge protection at panelboard LC1 in addition to the service entrance, and a building ground ring.
5.5 Standby power: on-site fuel for 96 hours at full load in the generator sub-base tank; outdoor sound-attenuated aluminum enclosure; bypass-isolation automatic transfer arrangement for the life-safety transfer switch ATS-L so it can be maintained without an outage; remote annunciator at the Staff Duty desk, Room 101.
5.6 Lighting: interior 3500 K; no color-critical visual tasks; standard catalogue luminaires (no samples); Training Room 140 uses the standard dimming range (no presentation dimming); egress and exit lighting on the generator life-safety branch.
5.7 Lightning protection is required.
6 Operation, maintenance and warranty
6.1 Acceptance testing by an independent NETA-accredited testing organization to NETA ATS.
6.2 Extended warranties (approved by the Contracting Officer, memorandum CO-4410-07): engine-generator set 5 years; automatic transfer switch 5 years; surge protective devices 5 years; LED luminaires 10 years; lighting poles 3 years.
6.3 Training: switchboard 4 hours; engine-generator set 8 hours; transfer switch 4 hours; lighting controls 4 hours.
7 Revision history
Rev B: conductor material changed to copper throughout; transformer requirements revised (efficiency basis, overload capacity for T-C1 only); fuel storage increased to 96 hours; interior CCT 3500 K; warranty periods updated; the 5-ohm grounding value of Rev A is withdrawn — grounding electrode system resistance is governed by IES-26.

 Where the model and a drawing disagree, report the discrepancy to the Contracting Officer before proceeding.

 4 Wiring

 4.1 Copper conductors only. 4.2 Insulation: feeders XHHW-2; branch circuits THHN/THWN-2.

 4.3 Phase identification: 480Y/277 V brown, orange, yellow, neutral gray; 208Y/120 V black, red, blue, neutral white.

 4.4 Metal-clad (MC) and armored (AC) cable are not permitted in new buildings.

 4.5 Raceways: EMT concealed and above ceilings; RMC exposed below 8 ft in mechanical and electrical rooms and
 exposed on building exteriors; PVC Schedule 40 underground and in slabs, with RMC or PVC-coated RMC elbows
 and risers; liquidtight flexible metal conduit for final connections to vibrating equipment, 6 ft maximum. ENT, LFNC
 and surface nonmetallic raceway are not permitted.

 4.6 Raceway fill. Where more than two conductors are installed in one raceway, the sum of the overall cross-sectional
 areas of the conductors must not exceed 40 percent of the interior cross-sectional area of the raceway. Take the
 conductor overall areas from the project conductor data sheet CDS-7 and the raceway interior areas from the project
 raceway data sheet RDS-1; the corresponding tables of NFPA 70 Chapter 9 are not reproduced in this standard and
 are cited by designation only. Install each parallel conductor set of a feeder in its own raceway; a feeder run must not
 carry more parallel sets than it has raceways. Count, in each raceway, three phase conductors, one neutral of the
 same size as the phase conductors, and one equipment grounding conductor. Size the equipment grounding
 conductor of a feeder the same size as the phase conductor where the phase conductor is smaller than 250 kcmil,
 and one size smaller than the phase conductor in the CDS-7 size list where the phase conductor is 250 kcmil or
 larger. Where a phase conductor is increased in size for voltage drop, increase the equipment grounding conductor
 by the same rule.

 4.7 Voltage drop. UFC 3-501-01 paragraph 3-2.7.1 governs and is adopted without change: 3 percent maximum for
 feeders and service conductors, 3 percent maximum for branch circuits, and 5 percent maximum total from the point
 of Government ownership to the furthest outlet. In addition, and more stringently, limit the voltage drop of any feeder
 of the emergency system to 2 percent of nominal voltage. A feeder is a feeder of the emergency system when it
 carries emergency system load, that is: the feeder from the normal source to the emergency system transfer switch;
 the feeder from the alternate (engine-generator) source to that same transfer switch; and every feeder on the load
 side of that transfer switch, including the primary and secondary feeders of any transformer serving emergency
 system load. The emergency system transfer switch is the transfer switch shown on the one-line diagram as serving

 IES-26 Fort Calder Installation Electrical Design Standard — Revision 4
 (February 2026)
 Directorate of Public Works, Engineering Division. Applies to all new construction on Fort Calder. Where this standard
 is more stringent than the Unified Facilities Criteria it governs; it never relaxes them.

 1 General

 1.3 No state or local electrical code amendments apply on the installation.

 1.4 Site conditions: inland; no salt-spray or corrosive areas. Cooling design dry bulb (0.4 %) 97 F (36 C); maximum
 recorded ambient 38 C; heating design dry bulb (99.6 %) 18 F (-8 C).

 1.5 The electrical coordination model issued with the contract drawings (50_bim/BLDG4410-E_RevC.ifc) is a contract
 document of equal standing with the drawings. Dimensions, equipment and luminaire locations, luminaire quantities
 and routed raceway lengths are taken from that model; they are not dimensioned or scheduled on the drawings.
 Where the model and a drawing disagree, report the discrepancy to the Contracting Officer before proceeding.

 4 Wiring

 4.1 Copper conductors only. 4.2 Insulation: feeders XHHW-2; branch circuits THHN/THWN-2.

 4.3 Phase identification: 480Y/277 V brown, orange, yellow, neutral gray; 208Y/120 V black, red, blue, neutral white.

 4.4 Metal-clad (MC) and armored (AC) cable are not permitted in new buildings.

 4.5 Raceways: EMT concealed and above ceilings; RMC exposed below 8 ft in mechanical and electrical rooms and
 exposed on building exteriors; PVC Schedule 40 underground and in slabs, with RMC or PVC-coated RMC elbows
 and risers; liquidtight flexible metal conduit for final connections to vibrating equipment, 6 ft maximum. ENT, LFNC
 and surface nonmetallic raceway are not permitted.

 4.6 Raceway fill. Where more than two conductors are installed in one raceway, the sum of the overall cross-sectional
 areas of the conductors must not exceed 40 percent of the interior cross-sectional area of the raceway. Take the
 conductor overall areas from the project conductor data sheet CDS-7 and the raceway interior areas from the project
 raceway data sheet RDS-1; the corresponding tables of NFPA 70 Chapter 9 are not reproduced in this standard and
 are cited by designation only. Install each parallel conductor set of a feeder in its own raceway; a feeder run must not
 carry more parallel sets than it has raceways. Count, in each raceway, three phase conductors, one neutral of the
 same size as the phase conductors, and one equipment grounding conductor. Size the equipment grounding
 conductor of a feeder the same size as the phase conductor where the phase conductor is smaller than 250 kcmil,
 and one size smaller than the phase conductor in the CDS-7 size list where the phase conductor is 250 kcmil or
 larger. Where a phase conductor is increased in size for voltage drop, increase the equipment grounding conductor
 by the same rule.

 4.7 Voltage drop. UFC 3-501-01 paragraph 3-2.7.1 governs and is adopted without change: 3 percent maximum for
 feeders and service conductors, 3 percent maximum for branch circuits, and 5 percent maximum total from the point
 of Government ownership to the furthest outlet. In addition, and more stringently, limit the voltage drop of any feeder
 of the emergency system to 2 percent of nominal voltage. A feeder is a feeder of the emergency system when it
 carries emergency system load, that is: the feeder from the normal source to the emergency system transfer switch;
 the feeder from the alternate (engine-generator) source to that same transfer switch; and every feeder on the load
 side of that transfer switch, including the primary and secondary feeders of any transformer serving emergency
 system load. The emergency system transfer switch is the transfer switch shown on the one-line diagram as serving
 NFPA 70 Article 700 loads. Feeders serving only optional standby (NFPA 70 Article 702) load are not feeders of the
 emergency system and keep the UFC allowance, as do the service conductors, which are not feeders. Calculate



Fort Calder DPW Page 1
 IES-26 Rev 4



 feeder voltage drop over the one-way routed length of the feeder.

 5 Distribution equipment

 5.1 Panelboards: copper bus, door-in-door hinged trim, bolt-on breakers.

 5.2 Surge protective devices: external units mounted adjacent to the protected equipment, 3 ft maximum lead length,
 with surge counter and Form C dry contacts.

 5.4 Nameplates: normal power black letters on white; emergency and standby power white letters on red.

 6 Grounding

 6.1 Building grounding electrode system resistance: 10 ohms maximum, measured by the fall-of-potential method.

 7 Seismic

 7.2 Designated seismic systems: the engine-generator set, the emergency (life-safety) transfer switch and distribution
 (ATS-L, T-E1, LE1) and emergency system raceways. Component importance factor Ip = 1.5 for designated seismic
 systems and 1.0 for other electrical components.

 8 Metering

 8.1 Advanced electric meter at the building main switchboard, Modbus TCP to the installation meter data
 management system (MDMS), 15-minute interval data. No other remote communication from the switchboard. Meter:
 three-phase 4-wire transformer-rated socket meter, Form 9S, ANSI C12.20 accuracy class 0.2, with test switch.
 Detailed ASHRAE 90.1 energy monitoring is not authorized.

 9 Testing

 9.1 Acceptance testing to NETA ATS by an independent NETA-accredited company with a NETA Level III lead
 technician. Scope: switchboard MSB; 480 V panelboards; dry-type transformers; feeders 100 A and larger (insulation
 resistance); grounding electrode system (fall-of-potential); SPDs; ground-fault protection on the main; generator and
 transfer switch (26 32 15 / 26 36 23 field tests witnessed).

 9.2 Power system studies are modelled in SKM PowerTools; deliver the native model files.

 10 Engine-generators and transfer switches

 10.1 Fuel: ultra-low-sulfur No. 2 diesel; biodiesel blends are not permitted. NFPA 110 designation: Class equal to the
 required on-site runtime in hours, Type 10, Level 1 for systems supplying NFPA 70 Article 700 loads.

 10.2 On-site fuel: 72 hours at full load minimum in a UL 142 double-wall sub-base tank with leak detection; the
 installation fuel delivery contract provides the remainder of seven days.

 10.3 Sound: 72 dBA maximum at 23 ft from the enclosure.

 10.4 Emissions: EPA-certified emergency stationary engine (40 CFR 60 Subpart IIII); covered by the installation air
 permit - no project air permit; the Contractor submits the EPA engine certificate to the installation environmental
 office.

 10.5 Field test: 4-hour resistive load bank test at 100 % of the nameplate kW rating.

 10.6 Transfer switches: 4-pole, open transition with in-phase monitor. Separate transfer switches for the emergency
 system (NFPA 70 Article 700) and for optional standby loads; the optional standby switch transfers 30 seconds after



Fort Calder DPW Page 2
 IES-26 Rev 4



 the emergency switch.

 10.7 Generator performance class: ISO 8528 class G2. Engine-generator transient performance is further limited for
 this installation as follows, and these limits are the project's requirement wherever the guide specification asks the
 designer to insert a value. On any load step of the step-load sequence, whether that step is the application or the
 rejection of load: the transient voltage dip must not exceed 15 percent of rated voltage; the set must recover to within
 2 percent of rated voltage within 3 seconds of the step; and the transient frequency deviation must not exceed 5
 percent of rated frequency. These limits are more stringent than the envelope quoted in the guide specification for
 engine-generator sets (which contemplates up to 30 percent voltage deviation and a recovery time of 3 to 5 seconds
 for a set taking full load in one step); the more stringent installation requirement governs. Demonstrate compliance by
 the step-load sequence prepared under the project's generator step-load basis, and verify it at the field test.

 11 Lighting

 11.1 Interior light sources: 4100 K maximum; CRI 80 minimum.

 11.2 Luminaire efficacy (FEMP-designated levels): troffers 120 lm/W, linear ambient 120 lm/W, downlights 90 lm/W,
 exterior area 105 lm/W minimum. Drivers: 0-10 V dimming.

 11.3 Lighting controls: stand-alone localized room controls; no networked or wireless lighting control system; no
 connection to the utility monitoring and control system.

 11.4 Exterior lighting: 3000 K maximum; CRI 70 minimum; parking-lot luminaires B2-U0-G2 maximum, wall packs
 B1-U0-G1; optical compartment IP66; driver surge protection 10 kV/10 kA; ANSI C136.41 7-pin receptacle on
 pole-mounted luminaires; aluminum anchor-base poles on concrete foundations; controls: astronomic time clock with
 photosensor, curfew dimming to 30 % from 23:00 to 05:00.

 11.5 Emergency lighting: 90 minutes.

 11.6 Interior illuminance targets. The values of the following table are the installation's design criteria for interior
 horizontal illuminance, by application. They are stated in the vocabulary of Section 26 51 00: 'Minimum Average' is an
 average, taken over the entire task area for the application, that may not be less than the stated value; 'Uniformity' is
 the ratio of the average calculated illuminance over the minimum calculated illuminance of the calculation grid, and

 IES-26 Fort Calder Installation Electrical Design Standard — Revision 4
 (February 2026)
 Directorate of Public Works, Engineering Division. Applies to all new construction on Fort Calder. Where this standard

 1 General

 1.3 No state or local electrical code amendments apply on the installation.

 1.4 Site conditions: inland; no salt-spray or corrosive areas. Cooling design dry bulb (0.4 %) 97 F (36 C); maximum
 recorded ambient 38 C; heating design dry bulb (99.6 %) 18 F (-8 C).

 1.5 The electrical coordination model issued with the contract drawings (50_bim/BLDG4410-E_RevC.ifc) is a contract
 document of equal standing with the drawings. Dimensions, equipment and luminaire locations, luminaire quantities
 and routed raceway lengths are taken from that model; they are not dimensioned or scheduled on the drawings.
 Where the model and a drawing disagree, report the discrepancy to the Contracting Officer before proceeding.

 4 Wiring

 4.1 Copper conductors only. 4.2 Insulation: feeders XHHW-2; branch circuits THHN/THWN-2.

 4.3 Phase identification: 480Y/277 V brown, orange, yellow, neutral gray; 208Y/120 V black, red, blue, neutral white.

 4.4 Metal-clad (MC) and armored (AC) cable are not permitted in new buildings.

 4.5 Raceways: EMT concealed and above ceilings; RMC exposed below 8 ft in mechanical and electrical rooms and
 exposed on building exteriors; PVC Schedule 40 underground and in slabs, with RMC or PVC-coated RMC elbows
 and risers; liquidtight flexible metal conduit for final connections to vibrating equipment, 6 ft maximum. ENT, LFNC
 and surface nonmetallic raceway are not permitted.

 4.6 Raceway fill. Where more than two conductors are installed in one raceway, the sum of the overall cross-sectional
 areas of the conductors must not exceed 40 percent of the interior cross-sectional area of the raceway. Take the
 conductor overall areas from the project conductor data sheet CDS-7 and the raceway interior areas from the project
 raceway data sheet RDS-1; the corresponding tables of NFPA 70 Chapter 9 are not reproduced in this standard and
 are cited by designation only. Install each parallel conductor set of a feeder in its own raceway; a feeder run must not
 carry more parallel sets than it has raceways. Count, in each raceway, three phase conductors, one neutral of the
 same size as the phase conductors, and one equipment grounding conductor. Size the equipment grounding
 conductor of a feeder the same size as the phase conductor where the phase conductor is smaller than 250 kcmil,
 and one size smaller than the phase conductor in the CDS-7 size list where the phase conductor is 250 kcmil or
 larger. Where a phase conductor is increased in size for voltage drop, increase the equipment grounding conductor
 by the same rule.

 4.7 Voltage drop. UFC 3-501-01 paragraph 3-2.7.1 governs and is adopted without change: 3 percent maximum for
 feeders and service conductors, 3 percent maximum for branch circuits, and 5 percent maximum total from the point
 of Government ownership to the furthest outlet. In addition, and more stringently, limit the voltage drop of any feeder
 of the emergency system to 2 percent of nominal voltage. A feeder is a feeder of the emergency system when it
 carries emergency system load, that is: the feeder from the normal source to the emergency system transfer switch;
 the feeder from the alternate (engine-generator) source to that same transfer switch; and every feeder on the load
 side of that transfer switch, including the primary and secondary feeders of any transformer serving emergency
 system load. The emergency system transfer switch is the transfer switch shown on the one-line diagram as serving
 NFPA 70 Article 700 loads. Feeders serving only optional standby (NFPA 70 Article 702) load are not feeders of the
 emergency system and keep the UFC allowance, as do the service conductors, which are not feeders. Calculate

 IES-26 Rev 4



 feeder voltage drop over the one-way routed length of the feeder.

 5 Distribution equipment

 5.1 Panelboards: copper bus, door-in-door hinged trim, bolt-on breakers.

 5.2 Surge protective devices: external units mounted adjacent to the protected equipment, 3 ft maximum lead length,
 with surge counter and Form C dry contacts.

 5.4 Nameplates: normal power black letters on white; emergency and standby power white letters on red.

 6 Grounding

 6.1 Building grounding electrode system resistance: 10 ohms maximum, measured by the fall-of-potential method.

 7 Seismic

 7.2 Designated seismic systems: the engine-generator set, the emergency (life-safety) transfer switch and distribution
 (ATS-L, T-E1, LE1) and emergency system raceways. Component importance factor Ip = 1.5 for designated seismic
 systems and 1.0 for other electrical components.

 8 Metering

 8.1 Advanced electric meter at the building main switchboard, Modbus TCP to the installation meter data
 management system (MDMS), 15-minute interval data. No other remote communication from the switchboard. Meter:
 three-phase 4-wire transformer-rated socket meter, Form 9S, ANSI C12.20 accuracy class 0.2, with test switch.
 Detailed ASHRAE 90.1 energy monitoring is not authorized.

 9 Testing

 9.1 Acceptance testing to NETA ATS by an independent NETA-accredited company with a NETA Level III lead
 technician. Scope: switchboard MSB; 480 V panelboards; dry-type transformers; feeders 100 A and larger (insulation
 resistance); grounding electrode system (fall-of-potential); SPDs; ground-fault protection on the main; generator and
 transfer switch (26 32 15 / 26 36 23 field tests witnessed).

 9.2 Power system studies are modelled in SKM PowerTools; deliver the native model files.

 10 Engine-generators and transfer switches

 10.1 Fuel: ultra-low-sulfur No. 2 diesel; biodiesel blends are not permitted. NFPA 110 designation: Class equal to the
 required on-site runtime in hours, Type 10, Level 1 for systems supplying NFPA 70 Article 700 loads.

 10.2 On-site fuel: 72 hours at full load minimum in a UL 142 double-wall sub-base tank with leak detection; the
 installation fuel delivery contract provides the remainder of seven days.

 10.3 Sound: 72 dBA maximum at 23 ft from the enclosure.

 10.4 Emissions: EPA-certified emergency stationary engine (40 CFR 60 Subpart IIII); covered by the installation air
 permit - no project air permit; the Contractor submits the EPA engine certificate to the installation environmental
 office.

 10.5 Field test: 4-hour resistive load bank test at 100 % of the nameplate kW rating.

 10.6 Transfer switches: 4-pole, open transition with in-phase monitor. Separate transfer switches for the emergency
 system (NFPA 70 Article 700) and for optional standby loads; the optional standby switch transfers 30 seconds after



Fort Calder DPW Page 2
 IES-26 Rev 4



 the emergency switch.

 10.7 Generator performance class: ISO 8528 class G2. Engine-generator transient performance is further limited for
 this installation as follows, and these limits are the project's requirement wherever the guide specification asks the
 designer to insert a value. On any load step of the step-load sequence, whether that step is the application or the
 rejection of load: the transient voltage dip must not exceed 15 percent of rated voltage; the set must recover to within
 2 percent of rated voltage within 3 seconds of the step; and the transient frequency deviation must not exceed 5
 percent of rated frequency. These limits are more stringent than the envelope quoted in the guide specification for
 engine-generator sets (which contemplates up to 30 percent voltage deviation and a recovery time of 3 to 5 seconds

 3. Voltage drop

 Calculate the line-to-line voltage drop of a three-phase feeder as

    VD (volts) = sqrt(3) x I x (R x cos(theta) + X x sin(theta)) x L / 1000 / N

 in which I is the design load of Table 1 in amperes; R and X are the alternating-current resistance at 75 C and the
 reactance, in ohms per 1000 feet, of one conductor of the selected size, read from conductor data sheet CDS-7; L is
 the one-way routed length in feet taken from the coordination model as described in paragraph 2; and N is the
 number of parallel conductor sets.

 The design power factor is 0.9 lagging for every feeder, so cos(theta) = 0.9 and sin(theta) = sqrt(1 - 0.9 x 0.9) =
 0.4359. Do not use a different power factor for individual feeders.

 Express the voltage drop as a percentage of the nominal line-to-line voltage of Table 1: VD (per cent) = 100 x VD
 (volts) / V(nominal). Compare that percentage with the allowance of IES-26 paragraph 4.7 for the feeder concerned.
 Each feeder is evaluated over its own length only; the cumulative check against the total allowance is made
 separately in the design basis workbook.

 4. Raceway fill

 Each parallel conductor set occupies one raceway of the feeder run. A feeder run therefore cannot carry more parallel
 sets than it has raceways; a design with more sets than the modelled run has raceways is infeasible and must be
 rejected.

 Each set consists of five conductors: three phase conductors, one full-size neutral of the same size as the phase
 conductors, and one equipment grounding conductor. Size the equipment grounding conductor by the rule of IES-26
 paragraph 4.6: the same size as the phase conductor where the phase conductor is smaller than 250 kcmil, and one
 size smaller than the phase conductor in the CDS-7 size list where the phase conductor is 250 kcmil or larger.

 The area occupied in one raceway is therefore

    A(occupied) = 4 x A(phase conductor) + 1 x A(equipment grounding conductor)

 using the overall areas of column 4 of CDS-7. The percentage fill of that raceway is 100 x A(occupied) / A(interior), in
 which A(interior) is the interior cross-sectional area of the raceway, read from raceway data sheet RDS-1 for the
 raceway material of Table 1 and the trade size shown in the coordination model. The limit is the percentage of IES-26
 paragraph 4.6.

def parse_dxf_texts(path):
    print('=== DXF:', path)
    with open(path, 'r', errors='replace') as f:

    i = 0
    texts = []
    while i < len(lines) - 1:
        code = lines[i]
        val = lines[i+1]
        if code == '0' and val in ('TEXT', 'MTEXT', 'ATTRIB'):
            entity = val
            layer = ''
            txt = []
            x, y = 0.0, 0.0
            i += 2
            while i < len(lines) - 1 and lines[i] != '0':
                c = lines[i]
                v = lines[i+1]
                if c == '8': layer = v
                elif c in ('1', '3'): txt.append(v)
                elif c == '10': x = float(v)
                elif c == '20': y = float(v)
                i += 2
            full_txt = ''.join(txt)
            if full_txt:
                texts.append((y, x, layer, full_txt))
        else:
            i += 2
    for y, x, layer, t in sorted(texts, key=lambda item: (-round(item[0], 1), round(item[1], 1))):

408:                  CHAPTER 2 GENERAL POWER SYSTEM CRITERIA
410: 2-1           VOLTAGE.
412: Refer to UFC 3-550-01 for voltage criteria associated with the primary distribution
413: supply voltage.
415: Unless there are specialty voltage requirements, base the facility system voltage on the
416: interior load requirements as follows:
418:        •      Apply 240/120V for facilities with only single-phase loads.
419:        •      Apply three-phase, four-wire, 208Y/120V systems for lighting and power
420:               demand loads less than 150 kVA.
421:        •      Apply three-phase, four-wire, 480Y/277V systems for lighting and power
422:               demand loads greater than 150 kVA unless 208Y/120V systems are
423:               shown to be more cost-effective. Use step-down transformers inside the
424:               facility as required to obtain lower voltages.
425:        •      For facilities with demand loads less than or equal to 150 kVA in which
426:               potential voltage drop issues have been identified, evaluate the life cycle
427:               cost effectiveness of installing larger conductor sizes and/or buck-boost
428:               transformers on a 208Y/120V system against the use of a 480Y/277V
429:               service utilizing step-down transformers. If determined that the life cycle
430:               cost is effective, the use of a 480Y/277V service shall be used in lieu of a
431:               208Y/120V service.
432: 2-2           FREQUENCY.
434: Apply a frequency of 60 Hz for distribution and utilization power.
436: In locations in which the commercially supplied frequency is other than 60 Hz, such as
437: 50 Hz, use the available supplied frequency to the extent practical. Where frequencies
438: other than that locally available are required for technical purposes, frequency
439: conversion or generation equipment can be installed. The facility user will normally
440: provide this equipment.

465:                CHAPTER 3 POWER DISTRIBUTION AND UTILIZATION
467: 3-1           TRANSFORMERS.
469: The transformer design criteria provided herein apply to interior applications and to dry-
470: type transformers fed by distribution traditionally placed in/for the facility downstream of
471: the main service. Most facilities will be supplied by an exterior utility system pad-
472: mounted transformer.
474: Interior transformers shall be sized according to the NEC.
476: 3-1.1         Low Voltage Transformers.
478: Specify dry-type transformers in accordance with NEMA ST 20 and the following:
480:         •     For transformers rated for 15 kVA or larger, use transformers with a 428
481:               degrees F (220 degree C) insulation system not to exceed a 239 degrees
482:               F (115 degree C) rise capable of carrying continuously 115 percent of
483:               nameplate kVA without exceeding insulation rating at a maximum ambient
484:               temperature of 104 degrees F (40 degrees C). Provide a transformer of
485:               80 degrees C temperature rise capable of carrying continuously 130
486:               percent of nameplate kVA without exceeding insulation rating when
487:               additional overload capacity is required.
488:         •     Transformers rated less than 15 kVA can use a 356 degrees F (180
489:               degree C) insulation system not to exceed an 176 degrees F (80 degree
490:               C) rise at a maximum ambient temperature of 104 degrees F (40 degrees
491:               C).
492:         •     When the transformer is located in areas where noise is a factor, specify
493:               sound levels at least 3 decibels below recommended values established
494:               by NEMA ST 20.
495:         •     Derate the transformer in accordance with the manufacturer’s guidance for
496:               locations with a maximum ambient temperature above 104 degrees F (40
497:               degrees C) and in accordance NEMA ST 20 for altitudes higher than
498:               3,300 feet (1,000 meters).
499: Include the following as part of the installation:
501:         •     Design system such that transformer vibrations are not transmitted to the
502:               surrounding structure. Small transformers can usually be solidly mounted
503:               on a reinforced concrete floor or wall. Flexible mounting will be necessary
504:               if the transformer is mounted to the structure in a normally low-ambient
505:               noise area.
506:         •     Use flexible couplings and conduit to minimize vibration transmission
507:               through the connection points.

514:                                                                         16 January 2025
515:                                                               Change 1, 21 January 2026
517:         •     Locate the transformer in spaces where the sound level is not increased
518:               by sound reflection. For example, in terms of sound emission, the least
519:               desirable transformer location is in a corner near the ceiling because the

# 1. Parse LM-63 IES files
def parse_ies(path):
    with open(path) as f:
        text = f.read()
    pos = text.find('TILT=NONE')
    nums = [float(x) for x in text[pos+9:].split()]
    # Line 1 after TILT=NONE:
    # 0: num_lamps, 1: lumens_per_lamp, 2: multiplier, 3: n_vert, 4: n_horiz, 5: photo_type, 6: units_type, 7: width, 8: length, 9: height
    # Line 2: 10: ballast_factor, 11: future_use, 12: input_watts
    n_vert = int(nums[3])
    n_horiz = int(nums[4])
    watts = nums[12]
    idx = 13
    v_angles = nums[idx:idx+n_vert]
    idx += n_vert
    h_angles = nums[idx:idx+n_horiz]
    idx += n_horiz
    candela = []
    for h in range(n_horiz):
        candela.append(nums[idx:idx+n_vert])
        idx += n_vert
    # Compute zonal flux per PCB-01 para 2:
    # a. Mean intensity at each vertical angle
    ibar = []
    for vi in range(n_vert):
        if n_horiz == 1:
            ibar.append(candela[0][vi])
        else:
            s = 0.0
            for hi in range(n_horiz - 1):
                a, b = h_angles[hi], h_angles[hi+1]
                s += 0.5 * (candela[hi][vi] + candela[hi+1][vi]) * (b - a)
            ibar.append(s / (h_angles[-1] - h_angles[0]))
    # b. Zonal sum
    flux = 0.0
    for vi in range(n_vert - 1):
        t1 = math.radians(v_angles[vi])
        t2 = math.radians(v_angles[vi+1])
        flux += 2.0 * math.pi * (math.cos(t1) - math.cos(t2)) * 0.5 * (ibar[vi] + ibar[vi+1])
    return {
        'v_angles': v_angles,
        'h_angles': h_angles,
        'candela': candela,
        'flux': flux,
        'watts': watts
    }

                             CHAPTER 1 INTRODUCTION

1-1          BACKGROUND.

Unified Facilities Guide Specifications (UFGS) are the set of standardized,
comprehensive specifications used by the DoD for designing and constructing facilities.
These specifications provide common requirements across DoD for safety,
sustainability, durability, and functionality and reference applicable consensus building
codes, DoD-defined requirements, and statutory and regulatory requirements. UFGS
ensure consistency, quality, and efficiency across various projects by providing a
standardized framework for a project team to use and edit for their project. These
specifications help streamline the specification process, reduce errors, and improve
communication among architects, engineers, contractors, and other stakeholders
involved in design and construction projects.

1-2          REISSUES AND CANCELS.

This UFS reissues and cancels UFC 1-300-02, Unified Facilities Guide Specifications
(UFGS) Format Standard, dated 1 April 2014 with Changes 1-3.

1-3          PURPOSE AND SCOPE.

This UFS provides guidance for the preparation of UFGS and establishes the general
content and format of UFGS and project specifications. Each DWG is responsible for
the technical content, format, and overall quality of their UFGS. Publication of UFGS is
available by electronic media, not proprietary, and at no cost to the user.

Preparers for both UFGS Masters and project specifications must use this UFS.
Specific guidance for each is provided as applicable.

1-4          APPLICABILITY.

This UFS follows the same applicability as UFC 1-200-01, paragraph 1.3 with no
exceptions, applying to all the government elements and contractors preparing UFGS
for DoD-owned Facilities.

1-5          REFERENCES.

APPENDIX B contains a list of references used in this document. The publication date
of the code or standard is not included in this document. Unless otherwise specified,
the most recent edition of the referenced publication applies.

                                                                   22 September 2025


                        CHAPTER 2 UFGS REQUIREMENTS

2-1          UFGS SECTION ORGANIZATION.

This paragraph describes the organization of a UFGS section.

2-1.1        Construction Specifications Institute (CSI).

CSI prescribes the use of three parts in each section and a consistent subject matter
sequence within each part. These recommendations are included in Appendix A and
must be followed to the extent practical in UFGS. When a part has no content, insert
"Not used." in the body of the text.

2-1.2        Table of Contents (TOC).

SpecsIntact has two options for printing the Table of Contents using the Print/Publish
function: 1) For the entire project or master, and 2) For the section. The Project or
Master TOC is printed as a separate document. The Section TOC is printed within the
section when the Combine Sections and Section TOC is selected. For instructions,
refer to the SpecsIntact eLearning modules found in Chapter 4: Process and
Print/Publish on the SpecsIntact website
(https://www.wbdg.org/dod/specsintact/elearning).

2-1.3        Attachments.

Attachments are files included at the end of an individual section Portable Document
Format (PDF). Section attachments (such as Figures and Forms) can be listed in the
Section TOC by using the attachment tag, <ATT>, around the attachment title in the
section text. For instructions, refer to the SpecsIntact Tags topic (ATT Tag) on the
SpecsIntact Web-based Help website
(https://www.wbdg.org/tools/specsintact/Help/index.htm).

2-1.4        Appendices.

Appendices are files included at the end of the specifications package PDF. Do not
attach appendices to individual specification sections.

2-2          CONTENT.

UFGS are for the purpose of translating design criteria into construction requirements
that have been coordinated with industry, thereby providing requirements for specifiers
to incorporate into construction contracts. Appendix A p
=== PART 2 ===
rovides the organizational
guidance for UFGS and recommends the approach to addressing content. Refer to the
SpecsIntact eLearning modules found in Chapter 7: Master Preparation on the
SpecsIntact website.




                                           2
                                                                           UFS 1-300-02
                                                                     22 September 2025


2-2.1         UFGS Master Content Guidance.

Write the UFGS Master in a clear, concise, complete, and correct manner. Reference
non-Government standards to the greatest extent possible in lieu of repeating their
requirements. UFGS are broad and non-geographical in technical content.

Provide bracketed or tailored options when requirements may vary. Accompany
bracketed or tailored options with designer notes to provide direction on identifying and
selecting the appropriate options. For example, when the selection of a material,
component, or system for corrosion prevention, life cycle cost effectiveness, or durability
depends on the location, application, conditions, or atmospheric and chemical
environment.

2-2.2         Editing UFGS for Projects.

Use the latest version of UFGS in accordance with UFC 1-200-01, paragraph 1-3 and
paragraph 1-6.3.3. The UFGS are master guide specifications that provide the
minimum level of quality. Do not specify lesser quality requirements than provided in
the UFGS. Edit the specification sections for project requirements. Add, modify, and
delete content as required for each project scope. Do not repeat requirements from the
drawings.

2-3           FORMAT.

The UFGS format is based on the Construction Specifications Institute (CSI)
SectionFormat™ and is designed for use with SpecsIntact software. Use of SpecsIntact
and the UFGS database is mandatory. SpecsIntact includes the UFGS Section
Template that complies with this UFS and can be used as a starting point for preparing
new UFGS sections. Specifications must be in UFGS format, comply with this UFS,
and be prepared in SpecsIntact.

2-3.1         Electronic File Format.

The UFGS Section Template provides the page layout, banners, notes, text paragraphs,
tables, fonts, page numbers, headers, and other basic elements of a UFGS.
SpecsIntact files are in Extensible Markup Language (XML) format with a SEC
extension. SpecsIntact can also publish UFGS in PDF using the SpecsIntact PDF
printer setting and Microsoft Word™ (.docx) formats. Download SpecsIntact through
your Agency’s software process or from the SpecsIntact website along with the PDF
SpecsIntact Installation Guide for setup and configuration instructions located on the
Support & Help Center on the SpecsIntact website. For additional assistance, refer to
the SpecsIntact eLearning modules, which provides instructions for its use.

The most current version of UFGS is available from the Whole Building Design Guide
(WBDG) DoD webpage (https://www.wbdg.org/dod/ufgs). Individual sections are
available in both PDF and SEC formats. The entire UFGS Master is available in SEC
format in a zipped file with the extension ZIP.

                                            3
                                                                           UFS 1-300-02
                                                                     22 September 2025


2-3.2        Section Numbering.

Each UFGS carries a unique section number and title in accordance with the CSI
MasterFormat®, Numbers & Titles (latest version). If a number listed in MasterFormat®
is used, then use its exact title as listed.

UFGS with the 5th level designator denote Agency-specific UFGS on the same
subjects: "10" for Army, "20" for Navy, and "30" for Air Force (for example, 01 78 24.00
10 is Army specific). These 5th level designators facilitate management of
specifications and provide identification within the WBDG and SpecsIntact.

2-3.3        Subpart Numbering.

Number subparts within the UFGS in accordance with the numeric system described in

                             CHAPTER 1 INTRODUCTION

1-1          BACKGROUND.

Unified Facilities Guide Specifications (UFGS) are the set of standardized,
comprehensive specifications used by the DoD for designing and constructing facilities.
These specifications provide common requirements across DoD for safety,
sustainability, durability, and functionality and reference applicable consensus building
codes, DoD-defined requirements, and statutory and regulatory requirements. UFGS
ensure consistency, quality, and efficiency across various projects by providing a
standardized framework for a project team to use and edit for their project. These
specifications help streamline the specification process, reduce errors, and improve
communication among architects, engineers, contractors, and other stakeholders
involved in design and construction projects.

1-2          REISSUES AND CANCELS.

This UFS reissues and cancels UFC 1-300-02, Unified Facilities Guide Specifications
(UFGS) Format Standard, dated 1 April 2014 with Changes 1-3.

1-3          PURPOSE AND SCOPE.

This UFS provides guidance for the preparation of UFGS and establishes the general
content and format of UFGS and project specifications. Each DWG is responsible for
the technical content, format, and overall quality of their UFGS. Publication of UFGS is
available by electronic media, not proprietary, and at no cost to the user.

Preparers for both UFGS Masters and project specifications must use this UFS.
Specific guidance for each is provided as applicable.

1-4          APPLICABILITY.

This UFS follows the same applicability as UFC 1-200-01, paragraph 1.3 with no
exceptions, applying to all the government elements and contractors preparing UFGS
for DoD-owned Facilities.

1-5          REFERENCES.

APPENDIX B contains a list of references used in this document. The publication date
of the code or standard is not included in this document. Unless otherwise specified,
the most recent edition of the referenced publication applies.

                        CHAPTER 2 UFGS REQUIREMENTS

2-1          UFGS SECTION ORGANIZATION.

This paragraph describes the organization of a UFGS section.

2-1.1        Construction Specifications Institute (CSI).

CSI prescribes the use of three parts in each section and a consistent subject matter
sequence within each part. These recommendations are included in Appendix A and
must be followed to the extent practical in UFGS. When a part has no content, insert
"Not used." in the body of the text.

2-1.2        Table of Contents (TOC).

SpecsIntact has two options for printing the Table of Contents using the Print/Publish
function: 1) For the entire project or master, and 2) For the section. The Project or
Master TOC is printed as a separate document. The Section TOC is printed within the
section when the Combine Sections and Section TOC is selected. For instructions,
refer to the SpecsIntact eLearning modules found in Chapter 4: Process and
Print/Publish on the SpecsIntact website
(https://www.wbdg.org/dod/specsintact/elearning).

2-1.3        Attachments.

Attachments are files included at the end of an individual section Portable Document
Format (PDF). Section attachments (such as Figures and Forms) can be listed in the
Section TOC by using the attachment tag, <ATT>, around the attachment title in the
section text. For instructions, refer to the SpecsIntact Tags topic (ATT Tag) on the
SpecsIntact Web-based Help website
(https://www.wbdg.org/tools/specsintact/Help/index.htm).

2-1.4        Appendices.

Appendices are files included at the end of the specifications package PDF. Do not
attach appendices to individual specification sections.

2-2          CONTENT.

UFGS are for the purpose of translating design criteria into construction requirements
that have been coordinated with industry, thereby providing requirements for specifiers
to incorporate into construction contracts. Appendix A provides the organizational
guidance for UFGS and recommends the approach to addressing content. Refer to the
SpecsIntact eLearning modules found in Chapter 7: Master Preparation on the
SpecsIntact website.

2-3.12.5      Submittal Item Reviewers.

2-3.12.5.1    Army.

brackets following a "G" on a submittal item indicate a specific Government reviewer
and approval is required for that item. For submittals requiring Government approval on
Army projects, a code of up to three characters within the submittal tags must follow the

Codes for Army projects are:

"AO" for Area Office
"RO" for Resident Office

2-3.12.5.2    Navy.

When the Naval Facilities Engineering Command is the Designated Construction Agent,
do not use the brackets following the “G”. For projects, edit UFGS 01 33 00, paragraph
Forwarding Submittals Requiring Government Approval, to designate who approves
Government Approved submittals.

2-3.12.6      Design-Build Submittals for Design after Award.

2-3.12.6.1    Army.

For Army only, when a "D" follows a submittal item, it indicates Designer of Record
Approval (DA) is required for that item. When a "C" follows a submittal item, it indicates
Government Conformance Review of Design (CR) is required for that item. When an
"R" follows a submittal item, it indicates both a Designer of Record Approval and
Government Conformance Review (DA/CR) are required for that item. When an "A"
follows a submittal item, it indicates both a Designer of Record Approval and
Government Approval (DA/GA) are required for that item.

2-3.12.6.2    Navy.

into O&M Manuals for the project. The requirements and format of the O&M Manuals

2-4           WRITING STYLE.

Write in a direct, active voice with simple, concise sentences. Avoid ambiguous,
indefinite terms such as "too short" or "relatively simple." Define what applies instead of
using "applicable" or other indefinite wording. Do not use "as shown on the drawings"
as this phrase is frequently overlooked. If used in a UFGS and the item is not shown on
the drawings, then the item is not specified. For additional guidance, see the Federal
Plain Language Guidelines (https://www.plainlanguage.gov/guidelines/).

2-4.1         Mood, Tense, and Voice.

Use the imperative mood (such as, Install equipment) except when clarity requires the
use of the indicative mood (such as, Equipment must).

Speak only to the Contractor, not the subcontractor, supplier, or manufacturer.
Directing the Contractor through these parties can be misinterpreted as indicating
responsibility. Stating "the manufacturer must provide," could be incorrectly interpreted
as informing the Contractor that a party other than the Contractor is responsible. It is
unnecessary to differentiate between the Contractor’s actions and the Contractor's
various suppliers, as this could be interpreted as assigning work. Do not use the
specification to instruct the Contracting Officer.

2-4.2         Abbreviations and Acronyms.

Use of abbreviations and acronyms must follow the practices within the discipline
involved. At the first use, write out the term completely and follow with the abbreviation
or acronym in parentheses. Use abbreviations for units such as psi, cfm, and kW, and
be consistent in their use.

2-4.3         Units.

Spell out numbers zero - nine, except units of time and measurement, and use
numerals for numbers 10 and above. Avoid starting a sentence with a number, but
when unavoidable, always spell out the number when it is the first word of a sentence.
Do not repeat a spelled-out number with a numeral in parentheses.

2-4.4       Terminology.

        •   The use of “shall” is prohibited. “Shall” imposes an obligation to act but
            may be confused with prediction of future action.
        •   Avoid the use of "must". If use cannot be avoided, use “must” to prescribe
            mandatory requirements, actions, and procedures. “Must” imposes
            obligation and indicates a necessity to act.
        •   Do not use the word "should" in the specification text for mandatory
            requirements as "should" implies a recommendation. "Should" may be in
            designer notes to indicate desirable procedures that are advisory in
            nature.
        •   Do not use “Contractor must provide”, use “Provide”. Project
            specifications are already directed to the Contractor, who is responsible

        •   Do not use the term "furnish" unless only delivery of material to the site is

            others will furnish equipment or materials and Contractor will install. Use
            "provide" to mean "furnish and install".

            Contractor. “To be” implies that someone will accomplish the work other

Subpart K—Distribution Transformers

Source:70 FR 60416, Oct. 18, 2005, unless otherwise noted.


§ 431.191 Purpose and scope.
This subpart contains energy conservation requirements for distribution transformers, pursuant to Parts B and C of Title III of the Energy Policy and Conservation Act, as amended, 42 U.S.C. 6291-6317.
[71 FR 24995, Apr. 27, 2006]




§ 431.192 Definitions.
The following definitions apply for purposes of this subpart:
Autotransformer means a transformer that:
(1) Has one physical winding that consists of a series winding part and a common winding part;
(2) Has no isolation between its primary and secondary circuits; and
(3) During step-down operation, has a primary voltage that is equal to the total of the series and common winding voltages, and a secondary voltage that is equal to the common winding voltage.
Auxiliary device means a localized component of a distribution transformer that is a circuit breaker, switch, fuse, or surge/lightning arrester.
Basic model means a group of models of distribution transformers manufactured by a single manufacturer, that have the same insulation type (i.e., liquid-immersed or dry-type), have the same number of phases (i.e., single or three), have the same standard kVA rating, and do not have any differentiating electrical, physical or functional features that affect energy consumption. Differences in voltage and differences in basic impulse insulation level (BIL) rating are examples of differentiating electrical features that affect energy consumption.
Distribution transformer means a transformer that—
(1) Has an input line voltage of 34.5 kV or less;
(2) Has an output line voltage of 600 V or less;
(3) Is rated for operation at a frequency of 60 Hz; and
(4) Has a capacity of 10 kVA to 5000 kVA for liquid-immersed units and 15 kVA to 5000 kVA for dry-type units; but
(5) The term “distribution transformer” does not include a transformer that is an—
(i) Autotransformer;
(ii) Drive (isolation) transformer;
(iii) Grounding transformer;
(iv) Machine-tool (control) transformer;
(v) Nonventilated transformer;
(vi) Rectifier transformer;
(vii) Regulating transformer;
(viii) Sealed transformer;
(ix) Special-impedance transformer;
(x) Testing transformer;
(xi) Transformer with tap range of 20 percent or more;
(xii) Uninterruptible power supply transformer; or
(xiii) Welding transformer.
Drive (isolation) transformer means a transformer that:
(1) Isolates an electric motor from the line;
(2) Accommodates the added loads of drive-created harmonics;
(3) Is designed to withstand the additional mechanical stresses resulting from an alternating current adjustable frequency motor drive or a direct current motor drive; and
(4) Has a rated output voltage that is neither “208Y/120” nor “480Y/277”.
Efficiency means the ratio of the useful power output to the total power input.
Excitation current or no-load current means the current that flows in any winding used to excite the transformer when all other windings are open-circuited.
Grounding transformer means a three-phase transformer intended primarily to provide a neutral point for system-grounding purposes, either by means of:
(1) A grounded wye primary winding and a delta secondary winding; or
(2) A transformer with its primary winding in a zig-zag winding arrangement, and with no secondary winding.
Liquid-immersed distribution transformer means a distribution transformer in which the core and coil assembly is immersed in an insulating liquid.
Load loss means, for a distribution transformer, those losses incident to a specified load carried by the transformer, including losses in the windings as well as stray losses in the conducting parts of the transformer.

§ 434.99 Explanation of numbering system for codes.
(a) For purposes of this part, a derivative of two different numbering systems will be used.
(1) For the purpose of designating a section, the system employed in the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) will be employed. The number “434” which signifies part 434 in chapter II of Title 10, Code of Federal Regulations, is used as a prefix for all section headings. The suffix is a two or three digit section number. For example the lighting section of the standards is designated § 434.401.
(2) Within each section, a numbering system common to many national voluntary consensus standards is used. A decimal system is used to denote paragraphs and subparagraphs within a section. For example, in § 434.401, “401.2.1” refers to subsection 401, paragraph 2, subparagraph 1.
(b) The hybrid numbering system is used for two purposes:
(1) The use of the Code of Federal Regulations' numbering system allows the researcher using the CFR easy access to the standards.
(2) The use of the second system allows the builder, designer, architect or engineer easy access because they are familiar to this system numbering. This system was chosen because of its commonality among the building industry.



Subpart A—Administration and Enforcement—General

§ 434.100 Purpose.
The provisions of this part provide minimum standards for energy efficiency for the design of new Federal commercial and multi-family high rise residential buildings, for which design for construction began before January 3, 2007. This rule is based upon the ASHRAE/IESNA Standard 90.1-1989 and addenda b, c, d, e, f, g, and i. (This document is available from the American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers, Inc., 1791 Tullie Circle NE, Atlanta, GA.) It is not incorporated by reference in this document, but is mentioned for informational purposes only.

General

§ 1910.301 Introduction.
This subpart addresses electrical safety requirements that are necessary for the practical safeguarding of employees in their workplaces and is divided into four major divisions as follows:
(a) Design safety standards for electrical systems. These regulations are contained in §§ 1910.302 through 1910.330. 1504:              General Voltage Drop Mitigation Strategies and Impacts.
1506: Voltage drop can be mitigated through various strategies, including increasing
1507: conductor size, reducing the circuit’s load, decreasing the conductor’s length,
1508: decreasing conductor temperature, and improving power factor. When establishing
1509: distribution equipment placement within a facility, locate panelboards relatively central
1510: to the loads supplied to minimize circuit lengths. Likewise, routing the majority of the
1511: distribution at 480/277V and stepping down to 208/120V more locally to the loads
1512: served will yield a lower voltage drop to the end devices; this strategy needs to evaluate
1513: a balance between transformer and circuit costs, as well as requirements to submeter
1514: different load types when applicable.
1516: Note increased conductor sizes will yield lower conductor resistances, lead to increased
1517: fault current values, and impact arc flash values at the equipment buses, potentially
1518: leading to protection coordination issues. Designers must ensure all conductor sizes
1519: are established prior to performing final fault current and arc flash calculations, and
1520: update safety calculations when modifying existing systems.
1522:              Voltage Drop Relationship with Utilization Voltage.
1524: Voltage drop calculations focus on energy loss through conductors, and voltage drop
1525: contributes to utilization voltage for end users. However, voltage drop and utilization
1526: voltage, which is the actual voltage seen at end-use devices and equipment, are not
1527: synonymous. Devices and equipment have acceptable utilization voltage ranges within
1528: which operation can occur, the lower bound of which can be of a lower voltage than
1529: yielded by the maximum permitted voltage drop alone. Other system losses occur
1530: throughout the distribution system, most notably through transformers, and the voltage
1531: delivered by the utility service may deviate from the nominal voltage assumed in
1532: calculations. Transformer tap settings aid in providing appropriate downstream
1533: utilization voltage, however, the use of transformer taps does not negate energy losses
1534: incurred through conductor impedance voltage drop.
1536: Design and construction personnel must remain cognizant of the utilization voltage
1537: requirements for the equipment and appliances served. Adjustments to the distribution
1538: system, such as the use of transformer taps and/or an increase in conductor sizes, must
1539: be performed accordingly to ensure proper utilization voltage is provided to the end use
1540: devices while simultaneously satisfying the voltage drop energy conservation
1541: requirements.
1543: Practices used to boost utilization voltage at the load must not be used as a method to
1544: comply with voltage drop requirements.

413:                                           INTRODUCTION
415: 1-1          BACKGROUND.
417: Unified Facilities Criteria (UFC) provide common requirements across DoD for safety,
418: sustainability, durability, and functionality for DoD facilities. UFC incorporate a
419: combination of consensus building codes, DoD-defined technical and user
420: requirements, and applicable statutory and regulatory requirements.
422: 1-2          PURPOSE AND SCOPE.
424: UFC 1-200-01 represents the foundational document of the UFC program in providing
425: general building requirements and overarching criteria, establishing the use of
426: consensus building codes and standards, establishing criteria implementation rules and
427: protocols (including core UFC), and identifying unique military criteria. In accordance
428: with the authority in MIL-STD-3007G, UFC are prepared by DoD committees called
429: Discipline Working Group (DWG), and are published by the Military Services under the
430: authority of the Engineering Senior Executive Panel (ESEP), comprised of the following:
432:         •    Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense (Construction) Office of the
433:              Secretary of Defense
434:         •    Chief, Engineering and Construction, Headquarters United States Army
435:              Corps of Engineers (HQ USACE)
436:         •    Chief Engineer, Naval Facilities Engineering Systems Command
437:              (NAVFAC)

439:              DCS/Logistics, Engineering & Force Protection (HAF/A4C)

444: modernization of DoD-owned and DoD-occupied facilities. It is applicable to all
445: methods of project delivery and levels of construction as defined below.
447: \4\ For temporary construction see paragraph 1-3.2.2, for non-permanent DoD facilities
448: in support of military operations see paragraph 1-3.2.3, for Host Nation Facilities see

cd /filesystem/final_batch4__electrical_task8_electrical_specs__blind && python3 -c "
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET

for sec in ['26 05 73', '26 20 00', '26 24 13', '26 32 15', '26 36 23', '26 51 00']:
    p = f'20_guide_specifications/UFGS_Division_26_SpecsIntact/{sec}.SEC'
    with open(p, 'rb') as f:
        root = ET.fromstring(f.read().decode('windows-1252'))
    scn = root.find('.//SCN').text
    stl = root.find('.//STL').text
    dte = root.find('.//DTE').text
    print(f'====================================')
    print(f'{scn} | {stl} | {dte}')
    for prt_idx, prt in enumerate(root.findall('PRT'), 1):
        pttl = prt.find('TTL').text
        print(f'  {pttl}')
        def walk_spt(el, prefix):
            for idx, spt in enumerate(el.findall('SPT'), 1):
                num = f'{prefix}.{idx}'
                ttl_el = spt.find('TTL')
                ttl = ''.join(ttl_el.itertext()) if ttl_el is not None else ''
                print(f'    {num} {ttl}')
                walk_spt(spt, num)
        walk_spt(prt, str(prt_idx))
"

import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET, re

for sec in ['26 20 00', '26 24 13', '26 32 15', '26 36 23', '26 51 00']:

    root = ET.fromstring(raw)

    print(f'=== {sec} ===')
    def walk(el, path=''):
        for idx, spt in enumerate(el.findall('SPT'), 1):
            p_str = f'{path}.{idx}' if path else str(idx)
            ttl = ''.join(spt.find('TTL').itertext()) if spt.find('TTL') is not None else ''
            # get text excluding NTE and child SPT
            txt_parts = []
            for child in spt:
                if child.tag not in ('SPT', 'NTE', 'TTL'):
                    txt_parts.append(''.join(child.itertext()))
            full_txt = re.sub(r'\s+', ' ', ' '.join(txt_parts)).strip()

                print(f'  {p_str} {ttl}:')
                # print sentences or bracketed chunks
                for m in re.finditer(r'[^.]*\[[^\]]*\][^.]*\.?', full_txt):
                    print('    ->', m.group(0).strip())
            walk(spt, p_str)
    for prt_idx, prt in enumerate(root.findall('PRT'), 1):

def write_xlsx(filepath, sheets_data):
    shared_strings = []

        if s not in ss_index:
            ss_index[s] = len(shared_strings)
            shared_strings.append(s)
        return ss_index[s]

    def col_letter(idx):
        res = ''
        n = idx + 1
        while n > 0:
            n, rem = divmod(n - 1, 26)
            res = chr(65 + rem) + res
        return res

    sheet_xmls = []
    for s_idx, (sname, rows) in enumerate(sheets_data, 1):

            '  <sheetData>'
        ]
        for r_idx, row in enumerate(rows, 1):
            lines.append(f'    <row r="{r_idx}">')
            for c_idx, val in enumerate(row):
                if val is None or val == '':
                    continue
                c_ref = f'{col_letter(c_idx)}{r_idx}'
                if isinstance(val, (int, float)) and not isinstance(val, bool):
                    lines.append(f'      <c r="{c_ref}"><v>{val}</v></c>')
                else:
                    s_val = str(val)
                    idx = get_ss_idx(s_val)
                    lines.append(f'      <c r="{c_ref}" t="s"><v>{idx}</v></c>')

        sheet_xmls.append((sname, '\n'.join(lines)))

    nums = [float(x) for x in text[pos+9:].split()]
    n_vert, n_horiz, watts = int(nums[3]), int(nums[4]), nums[12]

    v_angles = nums[idx:idx+n_vert]; idx += n_vert
    h_angles = nums[idx:idx+n_horiz]; idx += n_horiz
    candela = [nums[idx+h*n_vert:idx+(h+1)*n_vert] for h in range(n_horiz)]
    ibar = []
    for vi in range(n_vert):
        if n_horiz == 1: ibar.append(candela[0][vi])
        else:
            s = sum(0.5 * (candela[hi][vi] + candela[hi+1][vi]) * (h_angles[hi+1] - h_angles[hi]) for hi in range(n_horiz - 1))
            ibar.append(s / (h_angles[-1] - h_angles[0]))
    flux = sum(2.0 * math.pi * (math.cos(math.radians(v_angles[vi])) - math.cos(math.radians(v_angles[vi+1]))) * 0.5 * (ibar[vi] + ibar[vi+1]) for vi in range(n_vert - 1))
    return {'v': v_angles, 'h': h_angles, 'c': candela, 'flux': flux, 'watts': watts}

def interp_candela(lum, theta_deg, phi_deg):
    if theta_deg >= 90.0: return 0.0
    if theta_deg <= 0.0: theta_deg = 0.0
    v, h, c = lum['v'], lum['h'], lum['c']
    step = v[1] - v[0]
    vi = min(len(v) - 2, int(theta_deg // step))
    vf = (theta_deg - v[vi]) / step
    if len(h) == 1:
        return c[0][vi] * (1.0 - vf) + c[0][vi+1] * vf
    p = abs(phi_deg) % 180.0
    if p > 90.0: p = 180.0 - p
    hi = 0
    for idx in range(len(h) - 1):
        if h[idx] <= p <= h[idx+1]:
            hi = idx
            break
    hf = (p - h[hi]) / (h[hi+1] - h[hi]) if h[hi+1] > h[hi] else 0.0
    c0 = c[hi][vi] * (1.0 - vf) + c[hi][vi+1] * vf
    c1 = c[hi+1][vi] * (1.0 - vf) + c[hi+1][vi+1] * vf
    return c0 * (1.0 - hf) + c1 * hf
